question: A 55-year-old man underwent intracapsular cataract extraction (ICCE) decades ago and never received an IOL. He now attends clinic wearing thick aphakic spectacles. Which of the following optical distortions is he MOST LIKELY experiencing due to his aphakic spectacles?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Aphakic spectacles cause MAGNIFICATION (about 25–30%), leading to MACROPSIA (objects appear larger), not micropsia. Myopic spectacles cause minification.

answers.text: Approximately 25–30% image magnification (macropsia) and a peripheral ring scotoma

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. High-plus aphakic lenses (+10 D) cause: (1) ~25–30% image magnification (macropsia); (2) a peripheral ring scotoma (jack-in-the-box phenomenon) — objects disappear and re-appear as the patient moves their gaze through the lens periphery. These are intrinsic optical aberrations of thick convex lenses.

answers.text: Central scotoma with preservation of peripheral vision

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Aphakic spectacles do not cause a central scotoma. The ring scotoma (peripheral) is the classical aberration, caused by prismatic effect at the lens edge — the 'jack-in-the-box' phenomenon.

answers.text: Pin-cushion distortion with no effect on image size

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Pincushion distortion does occur with high-plus lenses but is not the most clinically significant problem. Image magnification and the peripheral ring scotoma are the primary disabling optical aberrations.

overallFeedback.feedback: Aphakic spectacles cause macropsia (image magnification ~25–30%) and a peripheral ring scotoma. This is why IOL implantation is always preferred — it corrects aphakia in situ with no image size distortion.

Correct. Aphakic spectacles → macropsia (25–30%) + peripheral ring scotoma (jack-in-the-box). These aberrations make bilateral aphakic spectacles tolerable but unilateral aphakic spectacles intolerable due to anisekonia.
